slides.title: Chapter 2: Riemannian Metrics
slides.notes: Frame the chapter as the moment a smooth manifold becomes a measurable space. Until a metric is chosen we have no lengths, no angles, no distances, and no notion of orthogonality. The plan today is to define the metric tensor cleanly, build a small library of standard examples, and then look at the structural operations: pullback, conformal change, products, and the indefinite analogue. By the end students should know exactly which geometric quantities the metric controls.

slides.title: The Riemannian Metric: A Pointwise Inner Product
slides.notes: Stress the parallel with linear algebra: at a single point the metric is just an inner product, and all the familiar consequences apply. The novelty is the word smoothly. The matrix entries depend on the point, and they vary as smooth functions in any chart. Positive definiteness must hold at every point, which is the property that fails for pseudo-Riemannian metrics later in the chapter. Mention that pure symmetry without positivity gives a much weaker structure.

slides.title: Three Foundational Examples
slides.notes: Anchor everything to these three families. The Euclidean metric is the constant case, where curvature computations vanish identically and everything reduces to linear algebra. The round sphere is the cleanest case of nontrivial constant curvature. The induced metric construction is the most important practically, because it produces almost every example we ever draw, surfaces, curves, level sets, and submanifolds of model spaces. Make sure students see that an inner product on the ambient space gives an inner product on every tangent subspace.

slides.title: Pullback Metrics and Isometries
slides.notes: The pullback construction is the engine behind almost every metric we will encounter outside of model spaces. The differential transports tangent vectors forward; the metric is then measured downstream and copied back. The positivity condition is exactly the immersion condition, which explains why local diffeomorphisms automatically pull metrics back to metrics. Isometries are the next abstraction: they are the morphisms that respect everything Riemannian geometry can see.

slides.title: Length of Curves and the Distance Function
slides.notes: This is the bridge from infinitesimal geometry to global geometry. The length functional is well defined because positivity of the metric ensures the integrand is real. The distance is then an infimum over all admissible curves, and the surprise is that this infimum recovers a genuine metric space structure compatible with the smooth topology. Caution students: the infimum may not be attained without a completeness hypothesis, which is the content of the Hopf-Rinow theorem later.

slides.title: Conformal Change: Rescaling Without Rotating
slides.notes: Conformal changes are the simplest deformation of a metric that still does something nontrivial. The pointwise scalar factor stretches all directions equally, so it preserves the angle measurement but distorts distance. This is also how the hyperbolic disk model is built from the Euclidean disk; the formula uses a conformal factor that blows up at the boundary. Set up the expectation that curvature will transform by a second-order PDE involving the scalar factor.

slides.title: Products and Warped Products
slides.notes: Products and warped products are the workhorses of constructing nontrivial examples. The direct sum metric is the obvious one and corresponds to placing the two factors at right angles. Warped products allow one factor to shrink or expand as you move in the other, and they capture surfaces of revolution and the standard models of constant curvature in geodesic polar coordinates. Encourage students to recognize the warping factor when reading a coordinate-form metric in the wild.

slides.title: Pseudo-Riemannian Metrics: Dropping Positivity
slides.notes: Replace positive definiteness with mere nondegeneracy and the geometry changes character. Vectors are now classified by causal type, and the unit sphere of the metric is a pair of hyperboloids cut out by a sign condition. The Minkowski model is the prototype, and almost every definition and theorem in Riemannian geometry has a pseudo-Riemannian analogue if one is careful about sign conventions. Note that distance no longer exists in the usual sense; one integrates proper time along timelike curves instead.

slides.title: Generalizations Beyond the Riemannian Setting
slides.notes: End the technical content by placing the Riemannian setting inside a larger landscape. Sub-Riemannian geometry restricts the directions in which the metric is even defined and is the natural framework for control theory and the Heisenberg group. Finsler geometry replaces inner products with fiberwise norms and allows direction-dependent speed. The pseudo-Riemannian world is essential for physics. Each of these generalizations sacrifices one of the clean Riemannian payoffs, which makes those payoffs easier to appreciate.

slides.title: What This Chapter Hands to Later Geometry
slides.notes: Close by emphasizing that the metric tensor is the smallest data set that turns a smooth manifold into a geometry. Connections, geodesics, and curvature in later chapters all take the metric as input. The operations introduced today, induced, pullback, conformal, product, warped, will recur constantly. The diagnostic question at the bottom is the habit students should carry forward: identify the construction, identify the signature, identify the isometry group, and only then start computing.
